entity.name: US FRONTIER Act
entity.desc: H.R. 9925, bipartisan House bill introduced Jul 23, 2026 (Obernolte, Trahan). Frontier models >10²⁶ FLOPs: published frameworks, annual third-party audits, 72-hour incident reports, licensed verifiers for the largest developers; up to $1M per violation. Would preempt state frontier-transparency, audit and incident-reporting rules.
entity.context: Would create a federal frontier-AI regime under a new Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security. Large frontier developers would have to publish, follow and annually audit a frontier AI framework and publish a transparency report at each deployment. Very large ones would also retain a licensed independent verification organization. The Commerce Secretary could order a halt to development or deployment that presents an imminent catastrophic risk. The preemption clause covers the ground of state laws such as SB 53 and RAISE (frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing, incident reporting) but leaves deployment, child-safety and state-procurement rules to the states. It is a congressional route to the national standard EO 14365 calls for, with binding duties the EO does not create.

cov.thresh: Frontier models trained with >10²⁶ FLOPs. Obligations scale with developer size: large (>$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI development spending over 36 months) and very large (>$5B and ≥$10B).
cov.eval: Annual independent compliance audits for large frontier developers. Very large developers retain a licensed independent verification organization for ongoing assessment of their framework, risk monitoring and mitigations, including internal use.
cov.timing: Transparency report before or at deployment of each new or substantially modified frontier model. Critical safety incidents reported within 72 hours (24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk to life).
cov.mit: Frontier AI frameworks must set risk thresholds, assess each model against them and decide on deployment and internal use; minimum framework requirements are set by regulation.
cov.sec: Frameworks must cover cybersecurity for non-public model weights; weight exfiltration is a reportable critical safety incident.
cov.halt: The Commerce Secretary may issue emergency orders suspending or restricting development, deployment or internal use of a frontier model that presents an imminent catastrophic risk.
cov.acct: Audit reports go to the Under Secretary, the Attorney General and opted-in state attorneys general. Civil penalties up to $1M per violation, enforced by the Attorney General and opted-in state AGs.
cov.update: Frameworks reviewed at least annually, with a justification published within 30 days of any material change; framework regulations reviewed yearly.

versions.why: The category definitions are the page's description of what each filter means; where they diverge from METR while citing METR, readers may take the map's broader categories for METR's.
versions.rationale: Compared each map definition with METR's component definition (metr-ce). Elicitation, weight security, halting, accountability (METR includes transparency, metr-ce#acct2) and updating match in meaning; thresholds, timing and mitigations are broadened; evaluations is the map's own addition.

evidence.supports: METR's timing element is about evaluations and their frequency

versions.uncertainty: The broadening is deliberate (gap:thresh contrasts eligibility and capability thresholds), so this is a framing choice, not a factual error.
versions.question: METR defines capability thresholds as 'Thresholds at which specific AI capabilities would pose severe risk and require new mitigations'; the map says 'Levels at which obligations or risks trigger', which also takes in regulatory eligibility thresholds (compute, revenue). METR's timing element is 'when and how often evaluations must be performed'; the map says 'When evaluations and obligations apply'. METR's deployment mitigations are 'access and model-level measures applied to prevent the unauthorized use of a model's dangerous capabilities'; the map says 'Refusals, monitoring, content controls'. 'Model evaluations' is not one of METR's nine. Options: (a) keep the map's broader definitions and say they are adapted (pairs with metr-taxonomy; recommended); (b) restore METR's meaning, e.g. thresh 'Capability levels that pose severe risk and require new mitigations', timing 'When and how often evaluations are performed', mit 'Access and model-level measures that prevent misuse of dangerous capabilities' — then coverage notes that rely on the broader meaning (e.g. compute-eligibility thresholds under thresh, obligation timing under timing, content moderation under mit) become stretches to mark; (c) METR wording plus a short adaptation note, e.g. thresh 'Capability levels that pose severe risk and require new mitigations (here also regulatory compute thresholds)'.

decision.note: Review page response 2026-10-10: 'Go with your recommendation' — (a) keep the map's broader category definitions, stated as adapted from METR (P-0107). No change.
